title: Unplug an electric car, hang the charger up and shut the charge-port door
instruction: Unplug the car, hang the charger up on its post, and close the car's charge-port door.
context: Every electric-car driver unplugs after each charge. A J1772 connector can't come out until its release button is held down, which lifts the latch's hook off the inlet's catch; yanking a latched connector damages the latch and the inlet. People with weak hands find this hard, and robotic charging needs it too. Then the heavy connector, on its cable, goes back in its holster and the port door is shut. Overlap: plug-a-charger tasks (ManiSkill, RLBench) and DataCenterBench's charger unplugging have no latch, weight or cable; an earlier holster task (#162, TK-K8TK3T) used a block in a tray; the accepted push-fit task (#662) also holds a release while pulling, but has no cable, holster or door.
setup: On the table, in front of the arms: a section of an electric car's rear quarter panel, dark blue painted steel, 60 cm wide, 45 cm tall and 2 cm thick, standing upright on two grey steel feet (20 x 4 x 2 cm) behind it. Its outer face is 44 cm in front of the arm bases, from 35 cm right to 25 cm left of the midline. In it, 5 cm right of the midline and 15 cm above the table (0.90 m above the floor), is the charge port: a 12 x 10 cm opening with a black plastic J1772 inlet (10 x 10 cm) whose face is 1 cm inside it. The inlet's socket is 47.8 mm square and 3.7 cm deep, with the latch's catch (a notch 8 mm wide, 11 mm long and 8 mm deep) in its top wall; the catch's front lip, which the latch's hook pulls on, is on a stiff spring along the socket's axis (20 N per mm, up to 4 mm). The port's door (dark blue, 12 x 10 cm, 4 mm thick) is hinged on its edge nearer the midline and stands 110 degrees open, toward the arms. A J1772 charging connector (black and grey plastic, 25 cm long, 15 cm tall, 5.7 cm wide, 0.54 kg; nose 4.38 cm across and 4 cm long; pistol grip below and behind its body) is plugged into the inlet with its latch closed. Along its top runs the latch lever, with a red release button (2.4 x 2 cm) 13.5 cm behind the nose's face; pressed 6.5 mm (about 3.6 N) it lifts the hook out of the catch. Its black rubber cable (14 mm across, 0.3 kg/m, 0.73 m long) drops from the grip to the table, runs back to 10 cm in front of the arm bases, right to 26 cm right of the midline and on to the foot of the charger post, where it is fixed. The post is grey steel, 8 x 8 cm and 55 cm tall on a 14 x 14 cm base plate, centred 44 cm in front of the arm bases and 46 cm right of the midline. On its face toward the arms is the connector's holster: a black plastic sleeve, 9 x 9 cm outside, with a 50 mm square socket 3 cm deep (a 14 mm slot in its top for the latch's hook) behind a mouth 64 mm tall whose sides flare over 4 cm to 9 cm apart, centred 20 cm above the table and opening toward the arms 36 cm in front of the arm bases. Everything is fixed except the connector with its cable, and the door.
scoring: The latch is closed while the button is pressed less than 6.5 mm. Score 0 if, at any time: the connector is pulled out against the closed latch with 40 N or more for 0.1 s (a yank: the force of the latch's hook on the inlet's catch, read from the catch's spring; in a real trial, from a luggage scale holding the inlet on a slide); or the connector is dropped (no hand holds it, it is in neither the inlet nor the holster, and its lowest point is 1 cm or less above the table). A hand holds the connector when its finger pads are 30-75 mm apart and each pad's face is within 6 mm of it; it has let go when every part of its pads is 2 cm or more away. Otherwise the levels build on each other: 0.25 when the button has been pressed 6.5 mm or more while the connector is home (nose 3 mm or less from its seat), or once the connector has come out of the inlet with no yank (its hook can only pass the catch when lowered); 0.5 when, after that, the connector's nose is 5 mm or more out of the inlet and a hand holds it; 0.75 when, also, it hangs in the holster (its nose's face 20 mm or more into the 40 mm deep holster, within the socket), no hand touches it and it has been still for 1 s (moving less than 1 mm); 1.0 when, also, the port door is shut (its free edge within 5 mm of the panel); this ends the trial with success. Doing nothing scores 0.
reset_notes: Plug the connector back in with its latch closed, lay its cable as at the start, and swing the door 110 degrees open. Run with -E object_jitter=0: the layout, the scoring and the demo depend on it. Real trials use an unpowered J1772 connector and inlet (no charger, no electricity): mount the inlet on a slide in the panel through a luggage scale along its axis to read the force on the latch.
fidelity: Real-size J1772 connector (boxes; square 43.8 mm nose; 0.54 kg) and inlet. The latch is a sprung lever whose hook drops into a catch in the inlet; its button force (3.6 N) is provisional, unmeasured. The catch's lip is on a stiff spring (20 N/mm) to measure pulls. 0.73 m of the 14 mm cable (0.3 kg/m) is 18 jointed segments fixed at the post; a real cable is 5-7.6 m. Flat 60 x 45 cm panel section; the door is a hinged flap with joint friction, no latch or spring. No electricity.
